chapters.giris: This chapter lays the foundation of the course: what does management mean, and what do managers do all day? In the first lesson you learn the four functions of management (P-O-L-C), the three levels of planning and how an organization's performance is measured. In the second lesson you look at the same topic from the side of the person: what types of managers exist, which roles they play according to Mintzberg, and which skills they need according to Katz. The two lessons complete each other: one explains what management is, the other explains who does it and how.
chapters.baglanti: This first chapter is a map of the chapters that follow. The Leading function in P-O-L-C opens up in Chapter 3 as leadership and power. Chapter 2 turns to the people you manage: their personality, their values and their attitudes toward work.
chapters.sinav: Chapter 1 is tested in Part 1 of the exam: 20 multiple-choice questions, 2 points each, testing recall. So you need to know the definitions and lists (the four functions, the three planning levels, Mintzberg's ten roles, Katz's three skills) completely and by their English names. Each of the two lessons is worth about 4 points.

okul.once: Skim the names of the four P-O-L-C functions and Mintzberg's three role groups once. Take this question to class: What does a manager really do all day, and what does a manager need in order to do it?
odak: Where the lecturer draws the line between Planning and Controlling
How long each of the three planning levels lasts and who does it
How Katz's skills change with the manager's level
Examples of line and staff managers
okul.sonra: First work through lesson c1a from start to finish and answer the question in every step; then move on to c1b. Read the trap lists of both lessons together, because the exam mixes up Mintzberg's and Katz's lists and the P-O-L-C functions. Finally, answer the unit questions, and for every question you get wrong, go back to the step it comes from.

chapters.giris: This chapter focuses on the people being managed. In the first lesson you see the lasting differences between people: the Big Five personality traits, other dimensions such as self-monitoring and self-efficacy, the limits of personality tests, and values. In the second lesson you move from these lasting differences to how people feel about their jobs and their companies: job satisfaction, organizational commitment, the sources that feed them such as justice and stress, how attitudes are measured, and the fit between a person and their setting. The link is simple: who you are largely decides where you will be happy.
chapters.baglanti: In Chapter 1 you defined management as getting things done through the efforts of other people; this chapter introduces those “other people”. Chapter 3 uses the same Big Five traits again, this time from the point of view of leadership, for example the link between extraversion and leadership.
chapters.sinav: Chapter 2 is tested in Part 1: 20 multiple-choice questions, 2 points each, testing recall. Most questions describe a person with a few adjectives and ask for the right concept. Each of the two lessons is worth about 4 points.

okul.once: Read the five letters of the Big Five and the definitions of job satisfaction and organizational commitment once. Take this question to class: Is a person's behaviour at work decided by their personality, or by the setting they are in?
odak: The workplace examples the lecturer gives for the OCEAN traits
Examples of the three types of organizational justice
The difference between Role ambiguity and role conflict
Examples of person-job fit and person-organization fit
okul.sonra: First work through lesson c2a from start to finish and answer the question in every step, then move on to c2b. Read the trap sections of both lessons side by side, because the mix-up between conscientiousness and organizational commitment links the two lessons. At the end, answer the unit questions and go back to the matching step for every mistake.

chapters.giris: This chapter goes deeper into the Leading function from Chapter 1. In the first lesson you learn what leadership is, formal and informal leaders, French and Raven's five sources of power, and the styles that describe how a leader uses power (Tannenbaum and Schmidt, Theory X and Y, Muczyk and Reimann). In the second lesson you move on to two early approaches in leadership research: the traits that make a leader a leader, and the behaviours leaders actually show. The main idea of the chapter is that leadership comes from influence, not from a title.
chapters.baglanti: The Leading function from Chapter 1 and the Big Five traits from Chapter 2 come together here: extraversion, conscientiousness and self-monitoring are linked to leadership. In the glossary, the leadership terms appear together under Chapters 3 and 4, so the foundation you build here is also used in the next chapter.
chapters.sinav: Chapter 3 is tested in Part 2: 15 short cases, 2 points each, testing understanding in a scenario. Knowing the definition is not enough; you have to link the clue in the case (is it a title, knowledge or admiration? handing out roles, or caring about feelings?) to the right concept. Each of the two lessons is worth about 4 points.

okul.once: Read the names of the five power sources and the definitions of task-oriented and people-oriented behaviour once. Take this question to class: How can someone with no title still guide a team?
odak: The difference between Position power and personal power
Which power creates commitment and which creates alienation
The assumptions of Theory X and Theory Y
The traits that Judge and colleagues found to be linked with leadership
Why the laissez-faire style has the worst record

Because this chapter comes as cases in the exam, try to find the clue word that gives the answer in each step's question. At the end, answer the unit questions and go back to the trap list for your mistakes.

lessons.neden: This lesson sets up the language for the rest of the course. In the exam you read a short situation and decide “which function is this?” or “which planning level is this?”. You answer these questions not by memorising, but by knowing which problem each concept solves.
hedefler: Explain the definition of management in your own words.
Tell apart the Planning, Organizing, Leading and Controlling functions in a scenario.
Match strategic, tactical and operational planning to their time span and manager level.
Explain triple bottom line, OCB and process loss with examples.
Compare the traditional and the contemporary management pyramid.

adimlar.baslik: What is management?
adimlar.anlatim:
If a café owner works alone, she is the one doing the work. The moment she hires five employees, other people do part of the work and her job changes. This is exactly where management begins. The textbook defines Management as “the art of getting things done through the efforts of other people”.

The key phrase in the definition is through the efforts of other people. A manager is not someone who does every task alone; a manager is someone who gets results through the work of others. The textbook's key-term version adds two things: solving problems creatively and reaching the organization's goals. So management is tied to a purpose, and it works through people.

In the exam, wrong options usually break this core: “do the important tasks yourself”, “own the company” or “control employees' personalities and private choices” are not management. Ownership is a legal status; management is an activity.
adimlar.ornek: In a student project group, if Elif prepares the whole presentation herself, she is a good worker, but she has not managed. When she shares out the tasks and makes sure everyone brings their part on time, she reaches the goal through the efforts of others. That is exactly the definition of Management.

soru.q: Kemal owns a bakery but has hired a manager, Ines, who gets the daily baking and sales done by guiding six employees. Who is doing management in the course's sense?
o: Ines, because she reaches goals through the efforts of others
Kemal, because owning the business makes him its manager
Neither, because management means doing key tasks yourself
Both equally, because everyone in the bakery manages it
soru.x: The correct answer is Ines: management is reaching goals through the efforts of others, and she is the one doing this. The most tempting wrong option is Kemal, but ownership is a legal status; it does not make anyone a manager unless they get work done through others.

adimlar.baslik: Planning and Organizing: goals and structure
adimlar.anlatim:
The four functions of management are known as the P-O-L-C framework: Planning, Organizing, Leading, Controlling. The order is not random; it follows the natural flow of work. First you decide where to go, then you build the setup that will get you there, then you get people moving, and finally you check whether you are on the right track.

Planning means setting goals and choosing the path to reach them. A good plan is not made in a vacuum: it needs environmental scanning, forecasting the future and making sound decisions. Vision and mission, building strategy, and goals and objectives all belong to this function.

Organizing means building a structure and assigning people so that the goals can be reached: who will do which job, and who will report to whom. Job design, organizational design, culture and social networks also belong here. An easy way to tell them apart: Planning answers “what and why”, Organizing answers “who and in what setup”. If a manager is sharing out the work again or redesigning jobs, she is not setting a new goal; she is changing the structure.
adimlar.ornek: The owner of a bicycle shop decides to start repairing electric bikes this summer and sets a revenue goal for the end of the year: this is Planning. Then he puts one mechanic on this work, splits the workbench in two and shares out the other employees' tasks again: this is Organizing, because the goal stays the same and only the setup that leads to it is built.

soru.q: The head nurse of a hospital ward splits the team into two shifts and gives each nurse a fixed group of patients so that the ward's new care targets can be met. Which function is she performing?
soru.x: The head nurse is not setting a new goal; she is building the structure and assigning people to tasks to reach a goal that already exists. This is Organizing. Planning looks tempting because targets are mentioned, but the targets are already set; what happens here is the division of work.

adimlar.baslik: Leading and Controlling: influence and correction
adimlar.anlatim:
The plan is made and the structure is built, but nothing happens if people do not get moving. Leading is the social and informal sources of influence you use to get others to act. The key word is informal: Leading is less about orders you give through your title and more about inspiring, motivating, communicating and keeping the team together. Leadership, decision making, communication, teams and motivation belong to this function.

Controlling means making sure performance does not drift from standards, and it has three steps: (1) set performance standards, (2) compare actual performance with the standards, (3) take corrective action if needed. Systems, processes and strategic human resource management belong here.

The exam's favourite mix-up is this: if a manager compares a result with a goal and takes a measure, it looks like planning, because something forward-looking is being done. But the action is triggered by a deviation, so it is Controlling. Leading and Organizing also get mixed up: Organizing deals with structure and tasks, while Leading affects people's willingness and energy.
adimlar.ornek: A football coach sets a goal of two goals per match at the start of the season. After five matches the team's average is one goal; the coach sees this and adds extra shooting practice. Because standard, comparison and correction all come together, this is Controlling. His speech that fires up the players in the dressing room before the match is Leading.

soru.q: A call-centre supervisor notices that the average waiting time has risen to six minutes against a three-minute standard, so she adds two staff to the peak hours. Which function is this?
soru.x: There is a standard (three minutes), actual performance (six minutes) is compared with it, and corrective action is taken: all three steps point to Controlling. Adding staff also looks like Organizing, but what starts the action is the drift from the standard, and the question asks about the response to that drift.

adimlar.baslik: The three levels of planning
adimlar.anlatim:
Planning does not happen at one level only, because in an organization different people think with different time horizons. The logic is simple: the higher up you are, the further and wider you look; the lower down you are, the more concrete and short-term your plans are. The plan at the upper level is the frame for the plan at the level below.

Strategic planning covers three years or more and is done by top management. It concerns the whole organization, draws on the mission and decides how the company will position itself against competitors; it does this based on a SWOT analysis.

Tactical planning covers one to three years and is the work of middle managers. It sets out the concrete tools to put the strategic plan into action.

Operational planning covers less than one year and is done by lower-level managers. It is the specific action steps that support the strategic and tactical plans: a weekly shift list or a monthly order schedule, for example.

To tell them apart in the exam, use three clues together: the time span, who makes the plan and how concrete the plan is. If you see “two years” and “middle manager”, it is tactical; if you see “next week”, it is operational.
adimlar.ornek: The board of an imaginary café chain decides to become the most eco-friendly coffee shop in the city within five years (Strategic planning). The regional manager turns this into a concrete two-year programme to switch all branches to recyclable cups (Tactical planning). The branch supervisor then draws up next month's order and training schedule (Operational planning).

soru.q: The marketing manager of a mid-sized shoe company, a middle manager, draws up an 18-month programme of campaigns to carry out the firm's new five-year positioning. Which planning level is this?
soru.x: Eighteen months falls between one and three years, the plan comes from a middle manager, and its purpose is to carry out an existing strategy: Tactical planning. Strategic planning is tempting because the five-year positioning is mentioned, but top management has already made that decision; the marketing manager is planning the tools to put it into action.

adimlar.baslik: Leadership, entrepreneurship and strategy
adimlar.anlatim:
The definitions of these three concepts are very similar, so in the exam they show up in each other's places. Focus on what each one describes.

Leadership is an act of influence that gets others to act, and it rests on social and informal sources of influence. It is no accident that this definition is almost the same as the Leading function: leadership is the core of the Leading function.

Entrepreneurship is creating new ventures by spotting opportunities (needs, wants, problems) and using or creating resources to put innovative ideas into action. A person who does this inside an existing organization is called an Intrapreneur: they do not start a new company; they launch a new product or business line in their own company. The logic is the same; only the place is different.

Strategy, according to Hambrick and Fredrickson, is a central, integrated and externally oriented concept of how an organization will reach its goals. The “externally oriented” part matters: strategy describes where you will stand against competitors and the market. In short: leadership is about people, entrepreneurship is about opportunity, and strategy is about the whole direction of the organization.
adimlar.ornek: Deniz works at an insurance company and notices a problem: customers cannot upload photos of damage through the app. She convinces her manager and sets up a small team inside the company to build this feature. Because she spots an opportunity and innovates by creating resources, she is an entrepreneur; because she does it inside her own company, she is an Intrapreneur.

soru.q: A software engineer at a large bank spots that small shop owners lack a simple invoicing app, gets a budget from her bosses and launches the product as a new unit inside the bank. She is best described as:
soru.x: She spots an opportunity and starts a new venture inside an existing organization, so she is an intrapreneur. “Independent entrepreneur” is the most tempting wrong answer: the entrepreneurial logic is the same, but that person would start their own new company; here the work stays inside the bank.

adimlar.baslik: Performance: organization, individual and group
adimlar.anlatim:
How do you decide whether an organization or an employee is “good”? This step explains performance at three levels.

At the organization level, the Triple bottom line measures performance not only by profit but in three dimensions: economic, social and environmental; in short, profit, people, planet. This idea is linked to CSR (corporate social responsibility): taking responsibility, beyond what the law requires, for your impact on customers, employees, communities and the environment.

At the individual level there are two kinds of performance. In-role performance is the productivity and quality your job requires. OCB (organizational citizenship behaviour) is voluntary behaviour that goes beyond your role and benefits the organization. The difference: if it is written in the job description, it is in-role; if it is done without anyone asking, it is OCB.

At the group level the rule is this: group performance equals the group's inputs minus Process loss. Process loss is anything in group interaction that blocks good problem solving: wasted arguments or an unclear division of work, for example. That is why five talented people in a badly working group can produce less than the sum of what each would produce alone.
adimlar.ornek: Burak works in a library and handles book returns, his own task, quickly and without errors: this is in-role performance. After his shift, without anyone asking, he teaches the new intern how the system works: this is OCB. The same library's four-person events team spends its meetings arguing about who will do what and cannot finish the poster in time: this is Process loss.

soru.q: An outdoor-gear company publishes one yearly report showing its profit, the number of local jobs it created and the tonnes of CO2 it saved. Which concept does this way of reporting reflect?
soru.x: Profit is the economic dimension, jobs are the social dimension and CO2 savings are the environmental dimension; together the three make up the Triple bottom line. OCB may be tempting because it sounds like good behaviour, but OCB is an individual's voluntary behaviour beyond their role, not a company's performance report.

adimlar.baslik: The traditional and the contemporary view
adimlar.anlatim:
Think of management as a pyramid. The Traditional view keeps the pyramid upright: top management at the peak, middle managers below, employees at the bottom. Decisions flow from the top down, and the employee's job is to follow instructions.

The Contemporary view turns the pyramid over: the upside-down pyramid. Customers are now at the top; next come the employees and other managers who serve them; top management is at the bottom, supporting and serving them. The logic: the person who really deals with the customer is the front-line employee, and management's job is to clear the way for that person.

The tool for this is Empowerment: enabling a person to think, to act, and to control their work and decisions on their own. An empowered employee does not wait for approval for every small problem. The textbook also names two trends of today: DEI and sustainability. In the exam, when you see “top managers support and serve employees, who serve the customers”, recognise the contemporary view.
adimlar.ornek: An imaginary hotel chain gives its receptionists the right to offer a free room upgrade to a guest who complains, without asking the manager. The manager's job is no longer to give approval but to give the receptionists training and tools. This is an example of the upside-down pyramid and Empowerment working together.

soru.q: At a chain of pharmacies, the regional directors say their job is to remove obstacles for store staff, and staff may solve customer problems without asking for approval. This best reflects:
o: The traditional top-down pyramid of control
Process loss caused by an unclear structure
soru.x: Top management serving employees, and employees being able to decide without waiting for approval, describe the contemporary upside-down pyramid together with empowerment. The traditional pyramid may be tempting because there are still regional directors, but there decisions come down from the top and the employee waits for approval.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Comparing results with goals and then taking action is planning.
tuzaklar.dogru: This is Controlling: standard, comparison, correction. If a deviation triggers the action, it is control.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Tactical planning covers less than a year and is the work of lower-level managers.
tuzaklar.dogru: Tactical is 1–3 years and middle managers. Concrete steps for less than a year are Operational planning.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Leading and Organizing are the same, since both deal with people.
tuzaklar.dogru: Organizing is structure, division of work and job design; Leading is getting people to act through informal influence.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Every good behaviour beyond the job description is in-role performance.
tuzaklar.dogru: If it is voluntary and beyond the role, it is OCB; in-role is only the productivity and quality the job requires.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The definitions of Strategy and Leadership can be used in place of each other.
tuzaklar.dogru: Strategy is an externally oriented, integrated concept of direction; Leadership is an act of influence that gets others to act.

Controlling has three steps: set a standard, compare, correct.
Strategic is 3+ years and top management; Tactical is 1–3 years and middle managers; Operational is under 1 year and lower-level managers.
An intrapreneur practises entrepreneurship inside an existing organization.

lessons.aklinda: P-O-L-C asks four questions in order: What will we do? Who will do it? How will we fire people up? Did it work? If you spot a deviation and correct it, it is always Controlling.

lessons.ad: Managers: Mintzberg's roles and Katz's skills
lessons.neden: You have learned what management is; now you look at the person who does it. The exam asks for very clear distinctions here: the role that passes information inside versus the one that passes it outside, the manager who contributes directly versus indirectly, and the skill needed at the top versus at the bottom. If you know the logic behind these distinctions, you can solve any situation.
hedefler: Tell apart seven types of managers by their area of responsibility.
Place Mintzberg's ten roles in three groups.
Separate the disseminator and spokesperson roles by the direction of information.
Match Katz's three skills to manager levels.
Use Mintzberg's list of roles without mixing it up with Katz's list of skills.

adimlar.baslik: Types of managers
adimlar.anlatim:
“Manager” is not one single job. The textbook groups managers by what they are responsible for, and the exam mostly asks about the pairs that look alike.

A Top manager is responsible for the organization's strategy; this person is the guardian of the vision and mission. A Functional manager is responsible for the effectiveness and efficiency of one area, such as accounting or marketing. A Supervisory / team manager coordinates a subgroup within a function or a cross-functional team. A Project manager plans, runs and closes a project.

Two important pairs remain. A Line manager runs a function that contributes directly to the product or service; the textbook's example is the Tide product manager at P&G. A Staff manager runs a function that creates indirect inputs, such as finance and accounting. Ask yourself: does this department produce the product itself, or does it support the people who make it? If it supports them, it is staff.

A General manager runs a clearly separate unit that earns revenue: a store, a business unit, a product line. The difference from a functional manager is that this person makes decisions across functions, not in one area only.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary ice-cream company, the production chief in the factory is a Line manager because he produces the product directly; the finance chief who handles payroll is a staff manager because she gives indirect support. The person who runs the company's shop in a seaside town, deciding on everything from sales to staff, is a General manager, because he is responsible for a whole unit that earns revenue.

soru.q: Omar runs one branch of a garden-centre chain. He decides on staffing, stock, local promotions and opening hours, and is judged on the branch's revenue. What type of manager is he?
soru.x: He runs a clearly separate unit that earns revenue (the branch) and makes decisions across functions, from staff to stock; this is a General manager. Functional manager is tempting, but that person would be responsible for one area only, for example only marketing.

adimlar.baslik: Mintzberg's roles: the Interpersonal group
adimlar.anlatim:
Mintzberg gathered the work managers do into ten managerial roles and split these roles into three groups: Interpersonal, Informational and Decisional. If you understand the logic of the groups, you do not need to memorise the roles: a manager first builds relationships with people, then gathers and shares information through these relationships, and then makes decisions with that information.

The Interpersonal group has three roles. The Figurehead represents the organization in formal and ceremonial duties: cutting a ribbon, giving a speech at a ceremony. The Leader role is about the relationship with employees: motivating and guiding them. This role matters at every level of management. The Liaison deals with peers and people outside their own unit or organization: building ties with other departments and with managers of other companies.

Figurehead and Liaison can be confused, because in both the manager meets people from outside. The difference is the purpose: the Figurehead does ceremonial representation, while the Liaison builds a network of ties that will be useful later.
adimlar.ornek: The chief physician of a hospital cuts the ribbon at the opening of the new children's ward: Figurehead. The next day she meets the chief physician of a nearby hospital and builds a tie for sharing beds in emergencies: Liaison. In the afternoon she talks with her tired assistants and encourages them: the leader role.

soru.q: The head of a city library joins a monthly breakfast with the heads of the local museum and theatre to build ties that may lead to joint projects. Which Mintzberg role is this?
soru.x: The library head is building a network with peers outside their own organization; this is Liaison. Figurehead looks tempting because it involves meeting the heads of other institutions, but there is no ceremony or formal representation; the goal is to build ties that may be useful later.

adimlar.baslik: The Informational group: where does information come from, and where does it go?
adimlar.anlatim:
Think of the three roles in the Informational group by the direction of information. Information either comes to the manager, goes from the manager into the organization, or goes from the manager out of the organization.

In the Monitor role, the manager receives and gathers information: reads reports, looks into complaints, follows trends in the industry. Information flows toward the manager.

In the Disseminator role, the manager passes information into the organization, for example to their own team. Coming out of a board meeting and explaining the decisions to the team is this role.

In the Spokesperson role, the manager passes the organization's information outside, to its environment: to the press, to the public. A press release or an interview belongs here.

These two are the exam's favourite trap: Disseminator goes inside, Spokesperson goes outside. A hint: “spokesperson” makes you think of a company spokesperson, and a spokesperson talks to the world. Do not confuse these roles with the Figurehead either: the Figurehead does not pass on information but represents the organization in ceremonies; the Spokesperson carries information.
adimlar.ornek: The manager of a bike-rental company reads customer reviews and competitors' prices in the morning (Monitor). At noon she explains the new pricing policy to her team (Disseminator). In the evening she gives a statement to the local newspaper about the company's new fleet of electric bikes (Spokesperson). Even when the information is the same, its direction creates three different roles.

soru.q: After a meeting with the city council, the manager of a public swimming pool gathers her lifeguards and explains the new safety rules the council agreed on. Which role is she playing?
soru.x: She takes information from outside and passes it into the organization, to her own team; this is Disseminator. Spokesperson is the most tempting wrong answer, but a spokesperson carries information in the opposite direction, from the organization to the outside, for example to the press or the public.

adimlar.baslik: The Decisional group and roles by level
adimlar.anlatim:
Once information is gathered, it is time to decide. The Decisional group has four roles, and each describes a different kind of decision.

In the Entrepreneur role, the manager starts change and opens new projects; the decision is triggered by an opportunity. The Disturbance handler responds to threats and crises; the decision is triggered by a problem and often comes unexpectedly. The Resource allocator decides where the organization will spend its effort: splitting budgets, assigning people to tasks. The Negotiator bargains on behalf of the organization.

To tell the Entrepreneur from the Disturbance handler, ask “who started the change?” If the manager starts something new by choice, it is Entrepreneur; if the manager responds to a threat from outside, it is Disturbance handler. Do not confuse this Entrepreneur role with the concept of entrepreneurship from lesson 1 either: here it only means a manager's role of starting change.

The roles do not carry the same weight at every level. For supervisors (lower-level managers), the Figurehead role is less important, while Disturbance handler and Negotiator are more important. The logic is clear: ceremonies are mostly done by top management, while daily disruptions and bargaining happen on the ground.
adimlar.ornek: The operator of a school canteen splits the year's budget between the menu, staff and equipment: Resource allocator. One morning the fridge breaks down, and before lunch he arranges cold products from another supplier: Disturbance handler. Then he bargains with that supplier for a yearly discount: negotiator. On his own initiative, he also opens a healthy-snack corner: entrepreneur.

soru.q: A flood damages the warehouse of an online bookshop, and the operations manager immediately rents temporary space and reroutes orders. Which Mintzberg role is she playing?
soru.x: She is not starting the change herself; she is responding fast to a threat from outside (the flood); this is Disturbance handler. Entrepreneur is tempting because a new setup is being built, but the Entrepreneur starts change by choice, based on an opportunity, and does not react to a crisis.

adimlar.baslik: Katz's three skills
adimlar.anlatim:
Mintzberg describes what a manager does; Katz asks what a manager must have to do it, and he names three skills.

Technical skills are knowledge and expertise in a specific field: being able to use a piece of equipment, a piece of software or a procedure. Lower-level managers need them most, because they are closest to where the work is done and need to be able to show the work to their teams.

Interpersonal skills (also called human skills) mean working with people, leading them and communicating with them. They are needed at every level, because every manager gets work done through the efforts of others; remember the definition of management.

Conceptual skills mean producing ideas and seeing the big picture: strategy, mission, policies. Top managers need them most.

The logic of the rule: the higher you go, the further you move from the work itself and the closer you get to the direction of the whole. So as you rise, you need more conceptual skills and fewer technical skills, while interpersonal skills stay necessary at every step.
adimlar.ornek: In a restaurant chain, shift leader Can shows a new employee the cleaning settings of the coffee machine: Technical skills. The chain's general manager thinks about which cities they will open in five years from now and what the brand will stand for: Conceptual skills. When both of them listen to their teams and motivate them, they use Interpersonal skills.

soru.q: A newly promoted regional director at a supermarket chain now spends her days on long-term expansion plans and company policy instead of checking tills. According to Katz, which skill has become most important for her?
soru.x: Long-term plans and company policy require seeing the big picture; according to Katz, the higher you rise, the more you need Conceptual skills. Interpersonal skills are a tempting wrong answer because they are needed at every level, but the skill that grows and stands out as you rise is the conceptual one.

adimlar.baslik: Do not mix up the two lists: Mintzberg and Katz
adimlar.anlatim:
This unit has lists that look alike, and the exam mixes them up on purpose. Most wrong options put another list in place of the right one.

Mintzberg's list is about roles, that is, what a manager does: Interpersonal, Informational, Decisional. Katz's list is about skills, that is, what a manager must have: Technical, Interpersonal, Conceptual. The word “interpersonal” appears in both lists, so look at all three words in the option. If you see “Informational” or “Decisional”, it is Mintzberg; if you see “Technical” or “Conceptual”, it is Katz.

There is also a parallel that links the two lists. Mintzberg's Leader role matters at every level; Katz's Interpersonal skills are needed at every level too. That is because both describe the core of management: getting work done with people. The things that change by level are different: in Katz, technical skill stands out at the bottom and conceptual skill at the top; in Mintzberg, the Figurehead role shrinks for supervisors, while Disturbance handler and Negotiator grow.

Finally, the four P-O-L-C functions and the three planning levels may also appear as wrong options. If the question says “roles”, look for Mintzberg; if it says “skills”, look for Katz; if it says “functions”, look for P-O-L-C.
adimlar.ornek: Think of Zeynep, the president of a student club. When she represents the club at the university's open-day fair, she plays one of Mintzberg's roles (figurehead). What helps her play that role well is one of Katz's skills: her ability to communicate easily with people (interpersonal skills). The role is the work she does; the skill is the ability that makes that work possible.

soru.q: A training brochure claims: 'Managers need three critical skill sets: interpersonal, informational and decisional.' What is wrong with this claim?
o: It lists Mintzberg's role groups instead of Katz's skills
It lists the P-O-L-C functions instead of Katz's skills
It lists Katz's skills instead of Mintzberg's role groups
It lists the planning levels instead of Mintzberg's roles
soru.x: Interpersonal, informational and decisional are Mintzberg's role groups; Katz's skill sets are technical, interpersonal and conceptual. The third option is tempting because it also says the two lists were swapped, but the direction is wrong: the brochure says “skills” and lists the role groups, so Mintzberg was written in place of Katz.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The Disseminator passes information to the press and the public.
tuzaklar.dogru: The Disseminator carries information inside, to the team. The one who carries it outside, to the press, is the Spokesperson.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Liaison means representing the organization at ceremonies.
tuzaklar.dogru: Ceremonies and formal representation are the Figurehead. The Liaison builds a network with people outside the unit.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Katz's skills are interpersonal, informational and decisional.
tuzaklar.dogru: These are Mintzberg's role groups. Katz's three skills are technical, interpersonal, conceptual; do not mix up the two lists.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The finance manager is a line manager because she runs critical work.
tuzaklar.dogru: Finance creates indirect inputs, so it is a staff function. Line means a direct contribution to the product or service.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The figurehead role is more important for supervisors.
tuzaklar.dogru: The opposite is true: for lower-level managers the figurehead role matters less, while the disturbance handler and negotiator roles matter more.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Negotiator is an informational role.
tuzaklar.dogru: Negotiator belongs to the decisional group; bargaining on behalf of the organization is a decision task.

ozet: Line contributes directly, staff indirectly; a general manager runs a unit that earns revenue.
Mintzberg: 10 roles, 3 groups (interpersonal, informational, decisional).
Interpersonal: figurehead, leader, liaison.
Informational: monitor (receives), disseminator (gives inside), spokesperson (gives outside).
Decisional group: the entrepreneur starts change, the disturbance handler deals with crises, the resource allocator splits the budget, the negotiator bargains.
For lower-level managers (supervisors), the figurehead role shrinks; crisis handling (disturbance handler) and bargaining (negotiator) grow.
Katz's skills: technical is needed most at the bottom, interpersonal at every level, conceptual most at the top.
The higher you rise, the more conceptual skill and the less technical skill you need.
lessons.aklinda: Build ties, gather information, make decisions: Mintzberg's three groups flow in this order. If information goes inside, it is the disseminator; if it goes outside, it is the spokesperson.
lessons.sinavda: It comes in Part 1 as multiple choice, worth about 4 points. Questions usually describe a short piece of manager behaviour and ask which Mintzberg role it is, or ask you to match Katz's skills to manager levels. You may also be asked to link each list name to its correct owner.

lessons.ad: Personality and values: the Big Five and beyond
lessons.neden: The people you manage are different from each other, and some of these differences come from personality. Knowing personality helps you understand who will shine in which job and who will struggle in which situation. In the exam you are asked to find the right trait from a description of how a person behaves.
hedefler: Explain the definition of personality and how stable it is.
Identify the right Big Five trait from a description of a person.
Show the difference between self-esteem and self-efficacy with an example.
Explain the limits of personality tests in hiring.
Separate values from personality and list Schwartz's ten values.

adimlar.baslik: What is personality, and when does it make a difference?
adimlar.anlatim:
Put two employees in the same job and you will see them behave differently: one writes everything in lists, the other keeps it in her head; one speaks in meetings, the other listens. We call the lasting ones among these differences personality.

Personality is a person's relatively stable patterns of feeling, thinking and behaving. Read “relatively stable” in both directions: personality does not change from one day to the next, but it can change slowly over a lifetime. So it is wrong to say “it is fixed in childhood and never changes”.

Personality is also not the only thing that shapes behaviour at work. The demands of the job shape behaviour too: in a job with strict rules, everyone behaves in a similar way. That is why personality makes the biggest difference in jobs with high autonomy; when people decide for themselves how to do the work, their own patterns show.

Also separate personality from its two neighbours in this chapter: personality describes how you behave, values describe what is important to you, and attitudes describe your opinions and feelings about a specific thing.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary call centre, every employee has to read the ready-made script on the screen, so quiet Mert and talkative Selin look almost the same. The difference shows when Selin moves to the same company's events team and starts planning her own work. As autonomy grows, Personality shows more in behaviour.

soru.q: Two new hires show very different working styles in a small design studio where they plan their own days, but behave almost identically on a tightly scripted assembly line. What does this illustrate?
o: Personality matters most in jobs with high autonomy
Personality is fixed in childhood and never changes
Job demands have no effect on behaviour at work
Personality and values are one and the same thing
soru.x: Personality differences show where people organise their own work and autonomy is high; in a job with strict rules, the demands of the job decide behaviour. The second option may be tempting, but the textbook says personality is relatively stable and can change slowly over a lifetime; besides, the scenario is not about change.

adimlar.baslik: Big Five: Openness and Conscientiousness
adimlar.anlatim:
The most common way to describe personality is the Big Five model. Its first letters spell OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Each one is a dimension that runs from one end to the other; people score lower or higher on each dimension.

Openness: being curious, original, intellectual, creative and open to new ideas. At work these people learn fast, adapt easily to change and are creative; on the other hand, they may get bored in routine jobs.

Conscientiousness: being organized, systematic, punctual, achievement-oriented and dependable. This is the only trait that predicts performance across all jobs, and it is the trait recruiters look for most. The logic is clear: whatever job you do, working in a planned way and keeping your word helps.

The trap the exam sets here is a play on words. The description “organized, dependable, meets deadlines” is Conscientiousness, not organizational commitment. Commitment is an emotional attitude toward one specific company; Conscientiousness is a personality trait a person carries into every setting.
adimlar.ornek: In a project group, Aylin comes to every meeting with an agenda, writes the tasks in a table and never misses a deadline: Conscientiousness. Another member of the group, Kaan, keeps trying new presentation tools and looks at the topic from an angle nobody else thought of, but he quickly gets bored of writing reports in the same format: Openness.

soru.q: A recruiter can test candidates on only one Big Five trait and wants the trait that best predicts performance whatever the job is. Which trait should she choose?
soru.x: Conscientiousness is the only Big Five trait that predicts performance across all jobs, and it is the trait recruiters look for most. Extraversion is a tempting wrong answer because it helps in sales and in management, but that is true only for some jobs.

adimlar.baslik: Big Five: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism
adimlar.anlatim:
Extraversion: being outgoing, talkative and sociable. These people are good in sales and as managers, because they get energy from dealing with people. The textbook also notes a side effect: more absenteeism.

Agreeableness: being likeable, tolerant, sensitive, trusting, kind and warm. These people help others. But because they avoid conflict, they take less part in change-oriented communication, that is, in questioning the way things are. This is the price of a good trait.

Neuroticism: being anxious, irritable, moody and emotionally unstable. Among the five traits, this is the only one where a high score is not wanted; high scorers are less happy and have lower career success.

Extraversion and Agreeableness are often confused, because both look like being “good with people”. The difference: Extraversion is about enjoying being among people, and Agreeableness is about treating people well. A quiet but very helpful person can have low Extraversion and high Agreeableness.
adimlar.ornek: At a gym, Ece at the reception chats with everyone and breaks the record for signing up new members: high Extraversion. The trainer Okan is quiet, but he helps everyone patiently and avoids arguments: high Agreeableness. Tolga in accounting walks around tense and moody for days because of one small mistake: high Neuroticism.

soru.q: In a project team, Lars is kind and helpful to everyone but never questions the team's flawed plan because he hates conflict. Which trait explains both his strength and this weakness?
soru.x: Being kind and helpful is the strong side of Agreeableness; avoiding conflict and staying away from change-oriented communication is its price. Extraversion is tempting because it makes you think of good relations with people, but Extraversion means being talkative and sociable, not being kind and avoiding conflict.

adimlar.baslik: Self-monitoring and proactive personality
adimlar.anlatim:
Beyond the Big Five, there are other personality dimensions that make a difference at work. The first two are about how a person responds to their surroundings.

Self-monitoring is how well you read a situation and how much you adjust your behaviour to it. High self-monitors are called “social chameleons”: they are formal in the boardroom, relaxed at the team dinner and warm with the customer. Low self-monitors are the same person in every setting.

Proactive personality is the tendency to fix what is wrong and to take initiative without being told. A proactive person who sees a broken process does not stop at complaining; they fix it.

The way to tell the two apart is to look at what changes. If the person changes their own behaviour to fit the setting, it is self-monitoring; if they act to change the setting, it is proactive personality. One adapts the self, the other fixes the world.
adimlar.ornek: At a language school, the teacher Nora is playful in the children's class and measured and formal in the business English lesson she gives to adults: high Self-monitoring. At the same school, the secretary Arda sees that a mistake in the registration form keeps misleading parents, and he redesigns the form without anyone asking: Proactive personality.

soru.q: A junior accountant notices that invoices are often paid twice, and without being asked she designs a simple check that stops the problem. Which personality dimension does this show?
soru.x: Noticing what is wrong and fixing it without being told is proactive personality. Self-monitoring is tempting because it also takes attention, but self-monitoring means adjusting your own behaviour to the setting; here the person changes the setting, that is, the process.

adimlar.baslik: Self-esteem and self-efficacy
adimlar.anlatim:
These two concepts share the same root, so the exam almost always asks about them together.

Self-esteem is your overall positive feelings about yourself. It is not about one task but about how you see yourself as a whole: “I am a person of worth.”

Self-efficacy is your belief that you can do a specific task successfully: “I can write this report.” The textbook stresses that, unlike other personality traits, it is task-specific. That is why the same person's self-efficacy can be high for one task and low for another.

Telling them apart is simple: is there a specific task in the question? If you see confidence that changes with the task, such as “I am good at Excel but bad at presentations”, it is self-efficacy; if you see an overall feeling, such as “I like myself in general”, it is self-esteem. Even someone with high self-esteem can feel low self-efficacy when faced with new software.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary veterinary clinic, the nurse Melis is someone who trusts herself in general and feels she has worth: high Self-esteem. Still, when the clinic buys a new X-ray machine, she is not sure she can use it correctly; when it comes to giving vaccinations, she trusts herself completely. This confidence that changes from task to task is Self-efficacy.

soru.q: Jonas feels good about himself in general, yet before leading his first client workshop he doubts he can pull it off. Which concept explains his doubt?
soru.x: The doubt is tied to a specific task, his first client workshop, so it is his task-specific self-efficacy that is low. Low self-esteem is tempting, but the scenario says Jonas feels good about himself in general, so overall self-esteem is not the problem.

adimlar.baslik: Personality tests in hiring
adimlar.anlatim:
If personality tells you this much, using personality tests in hiring seems to make sense. The textbook is careful here and describes this use as controversial. There are three reasons.

First, candidates can fake their answers: someone who guesses what the job is looking for can present themselves as more organized than they are. Second, personality explains only about 10–15% of job performance; so most of performance comes from other things. Third, there is a better predictor: cognitive ability (general mental ability) predicts performance better than personality does.

There is also an ethical and legal condition: tests must not discriminate.

Do not see this as a contradiction with Conscientiousness “predicting performance across all jobs”. Conscientiousness is the most consistent predictor among personality traits, but the total explaining power of personality is still limited. In the exam, options such as “personality is the strongest predictor” or “tests cannot be faked” are wrong.
adimlar.ornek: An imaginary logistics firm chooses its warehouse supervisor with a personality test only and hires the candidate who looks the most “organized”. The candidate presented himself in the test as more organized than he is, and he struggles in the job. For the next hire the firm adds a cognitive ability test as well, because cognitive ability predicts performance better.

soru.q: An HR director wants to hire warehouse planners using only a personality questionnaire. Based on the course, which advice should she get?
o: Add a cognitive ability test, as it predicts performance better
Rely on the questionnaire, as candidates cannot fake the answers
Rely on the questionnaire, as personality explains most performance
Drop all testing, as no test predicts job performance at all
soru.x: According to the textbook, personality explains only about 10–15% of performance, answers can be faked, and cognitive ability predicts better. “Personality explains most performance” is tempting because Conscientiousness is a strong predictor, but the total explaining power of personality is limited.

adimlar.baslik: Values
adimlar.anlatim:
Personality describes how you behave; Values describe what you want in life. The textbook defines values as people's stable life goals, that is, the things that matter most to them. Like personality, values are stable, but unlike personality they point in a direction: what are you working for?

Values matter at two points in working life: which job you choose and whether you stay in it. A person who values security may choose a stable job; a person who values excitement may choose a setting that keeps changing.

The textbook lists Schwartz's ten values: achievement, benevolence, conformity, hedonism, power, security, self-direction, stimulation, tradition and universalism.

Do not confuse these values with the Big Five: benevolence is a goal (wanting the good of others), while agreeableness is a tendency in behaviour (being kind and helpful). Values are also the basis of person-organization fit, a concept you will see in the next lesson.
adimlar.ornek: Two friends who graduated in architecture are looking for jobs. For Selim the most important thing is security, and he chooses a long-established municipal office. For Defne the most important thing is self-direction; she joins a small studio where she can choose her own projects, and she stays there even when she is offered a higher salary. Values decide the choice each of them makes.

soru.q: Mira turns down a higher-paid corporate job to work for a small animal-rescue charity, because helping others is what matters most to her in life. Which concept best explains her choice?
soru.x: The goal she sees as most important in life, helping others, decides her choice of job; this is what values do. The other concepts in the options are personality traits or task-specific beliefs; what is described here is a life goal, not a tendency in behaviour.

tuzaklar.yanlis: “Organized, dependable, meets deadlines” is organizational commitment.
tuzaklar.dogru: This is a personality trait: Conscientiousness. Commitment is emotional attachment to the company.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Self-efficacy and self-esteem are the same thing.
tuzaklar.dogru: Self-efficacy is specific to one task; self-esteem is your overall feeling about yourself.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A high score is good on all of the Big Five.
tuzaklar.dogru: A high score on Neuroticism is not wanted; high scorers are less happy and less successful in their careers.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Personality is the strongest predictor of job performance.
tuzaklar.dogru: Personality explains only about 10–15% of it; cognitive ability predicts better.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Personality is fixed in childhood.
tuzaklar.dogru: Personality is relatively stable, but it can change slowly over a lifetime.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Self-monitoring means seeing what is wrong and fixing it.
tuzaklar.dogru: That is Proactive personality. Self-monitoring means fitting your behaviour to the setting.

ozet: Personality: relatively stable patterns of feeling, thinking and behaving; it matters most in jobs with autonomy.
The first letters of the Big Five spell OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism; name all five in order.
Conscientiousness is the only trait that predicts performance across all jobs.
Neuroticism is the only trait where a high score is not wanted.
Agreeableness is helpful but avoids conflict.
Self-monitoring adapts the self; proactive personality fixes the setting.
Self-efficacy is task-specific; self-esteem is general.
Personality tests are controversial: they can be faked and explain only 10–15% of performance.
Values are stable life goals; Schwartz lists ten values.
lessons.aklinda: Spell OCEAN, hire for C, steer clear of N. Self-efficacy says “I can do this task”; self-esteem says “I am fine as I am”.
lessons.sinavda: It comes in Part 1 as multiple-choice questions worth about 4 points. The most typical question describes a person with a few adjectives and asks which Big Five trait it is; the difference between self-esteem and self-efficacy and the limits of personality tests are also asked often.

lessons.neden: Personality describes who you are; attitudes describe how you feel about your job and your company. For a manager the real question is this: why do people stay satisfied, and why do they leave? This lesson breaks the answer to that question into parts and makes clear the fine differences you meet in the exam between types of justice, sources of stress and types of fit.
hedefler: Explain the difference between job satisfaction and organizational commitment.
Tell apart the three types of organizational justice in a scenario.
Separate role ambiguity from role conflict with an example.
Explain why attitudes predict intentions better than behaviour.
Match person-job fit and person-organization fit to the right situation.

adimlar.baslik: Attitude, job satisfaction and organizational commitment
adimlar.anlatim:
Personality is what you carry everywhere; an attitude is what you think and feel about a specific thing. An Attitude is our opinions, beliefs and feelings about aspects of our environment. Two attitudes stand out in working life.

Job satisfaction is the feelings people have toward their jobs, and it is probably the most studied attitude. Its target is the job: the tasks you do and your working conditions.

Organizational commitment is the emotional attachment people feel toward the company. A committed employee believes in the company's values, makes an effort and wants to stay. Even the language changes: instead of “the company's”, they say “our great benefits”.

The difference between the two is the target. Someone who does not like their job can be committed to their company (“my job is boring, but I believe in this organization”); someone who loves their job may not be committed to their company at all. In the exam, if you see the phrase “emotional attachment to the company”, the answer is commitment, not satisfaction. Do not confuse commitment with Conscientiousness either: that is a personality trait carried into every setting, while commitment is an attitude toward one specific company.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary zoo, the keeper Emre loves working with animals but complains about the shifts; so his Job satisfaction is mixed. Still, when a better offer comes from somewhere else, he says “we protect endangered species here” and stays. This emotional bond with the mission of the organization is Organizational commitment.

soru.q: A nurse finds her daily tasks dull, but she believes deeply in her hospital's mission, talks about “our patients” and refuses offers from other hospitals. What does she show?
o: High organizational commitment despite low job satisfaction
High job satisfaction despite low organizational commitment
High conscientiousness despite low job satisfaction
Low organizational commitment and low job satisfaction
soru.x: Finding her tasks dull shows that job satisfaction is low; believing in the mission, saying “our” and wanting to stay show that commitment is high. The second option is tempting because it swaps the two attitudes; satisfaction is the attitude toward the job, commitment is the attitude toward the company.

adimlar.baslik: Sources of positive attitudes
adimlar.anlatim:
A manager cannot change attitudes by giving orders, but a manager can change the conditions that feed attitudes. The textbook lists six sources; in this step you will see four of them, and in the next two steps justice and stress.

Personality & values: some people are satisfied more easily; for example, people with a low neuroticism score are more satisfied.

Job characteristics: skill variety, autonomy, feedback and meaningful tasks. These matter most for people with a high need for growth; someone who wants to learn and grow quickly loses interest in a monotonous job.

The Psychological contract is the unspoken, informal understanding of what the employee gives (effort, loyalty) and what they get in return (pay, raises, job security). Do not confuse it with the employment contract you sign: the psychological contract is not written anywhere, but when it is broken the employee feels cheated and their attitudes get worse.

Relationships at work: the relationship with co-workers and especially with the manager. Relationship management means communicating openly, keeping good relationships and managing conflict.
adimlar.ornek: At a software company, Elif has stayed late for years because she thinks her loyalty will be rewarded with a promotion; nobody ever told her this in writing. When the promotion goes to someone else, she feels deceived and her satisfaction drops. What was broken is not the employment contract but the Psychological contract.

soru.q: For years a chef worked unpaid extra hours, silently expecting job security in return. When the restaurant cut his hours anyway, he felt betrayed. What was violated?
soru.x: The expectation of job security in return for extra hours was not written anywhere; this unspoken understanding is the psychological contract, and the feeling of betrayal came because it was broken. The written employment contract is the most tempting wrong answer, but the scenario clearly says the expectation was silent, that is, unwritten.

adimlar.baslik: Organizational justice: three types of justice
adimlar.anlatim:
Organizational justice is whether employees feel they are treated fairly in the company. The textbook says trust lies at its root: an employee who feels unfairly treated does not trust the company. You can look for justice in three separate places, and the exam asks about exactly this distinction.

Distributive justice is the fairness of the outcomes received, that is, the rewards: pay, bonuses, raises. Its question is “what did I get?”

Procedural justice is the fairness of the methods used to make decisions. Its question is “how was the decision made?” If promotions are given out by drawing lots or by criteria that are never explained, this justice is damaged.

Interactional justice is being treated with respect, kindness and dignity. Its question is “how was I treated?”

The three are independent of each other, so find which one is broken in the scenario. For someone who gets a raise but gets it with a humiliating remark, the outcome may be fair, but interactional justice is damaged. If a fair salary is set through a secret and arbitrary process, the problem is in the procedure.
adimlar.ornek: At a hotel, the “employee of the month” award is given as the manager pleases, with no criteria explained: Procedural justice is damaged. At the same hotel, two receptionists learn that one of them earns less although they do the same job: Distributive justice. The manager tells off a waiter in front of the guests: Interactional justice.

soru.q: Staff at a bike courier firm agree that their bonuses are fair in size, but are angry because the bonus rules are kept secret and changed without explanation. Which type of justice is lacking?
soru.x: The size of the bonuses is accepted as fair; the problem is that the rules are kept secret and changed without explanation, that is, the method of deciding. This is Procedural justice. Distributive justice is tempting because the topic is bonuses, but distributive justice is about the outcome itself, and the staff already find the outcome fair.

adimlar.baslik: Stress: role ambiguity and role conflict
adimlar.anlatim:
The last source that affects attitudes is stress. The textbook splits the sources of stress (stressors) into three types: environmental, interpersonal and organizational. The general rule is simple: as stress goes up, satisfaction goes down. But there is one exception: challenging stress, for example an exciting and difficult goal, can also be positive.

Two of the organizational stressors are asked about in the exam in particular, and their names are very similar.

Role ambiguity is not being sure what your responsibilities are. The problem is a lack of information: nobody has told you where your job begins and ends. This is the employee who asks after a restructuring, “what am I doing now?”

Role conflict is demands that contradict each other, either within the job or between the job and other roles. The demands are clear, but you cannot meet both at the same time. Two managers giving opposite instructions, or an evening meeting that clashes with the time you pick up your child from school, are examples.

A quick test: “I do not know what to do” is ambiguity; “I know what to do, but I cannot do both” is conflict.
adimlar.ornek: At a festival organising company, the volunteer coordinator Ada does not know, after two teams merge, whether the ticket work now belongs to her or to someone else: Role ambiguity. At the same company, one of Bora's managers wants him to cut costs, and the other wants him to make the stage bigger: Role conflict.

soru.q: A lab technician is told by the research head to run every test twice for accuracy, while the operations head insists that each test is run only once to save time. What is she experiencing?
soru.x: Both demands are clear, but they contradict each other and cannot both be met at the same time; this is Role conflict. Role ambiguity is tempting because the technician seems confused, but ambiguity means not knowing your responsibilities; here the demands are perfectly clear.

adimlar.baslik: Measuring attitudes and the limit of attitudes
adimlar.anlatim:
A manager wants to measure how employees feel instead of guessing. The textbook names two tools.

Attitude surveys are questions asked to employees on a regular basis. They work best under two conditions: when the answers are kept confidential, because only then do people answer honestly; and when action follows, because if nothing changes, employees will not take the next survey seriously.

An Exit interview is a meeting with an employee who is leaving, held to learn why they are leaving. The difference from a survey is whose voice it collects: a survey collects the voice of those who stay, an exit interview the voice of those who go.

One last important point: attitudes are better at predicting intentions than actual behaviour. An unhappy employee intends to leave, but whether they really leave depends on their alternatives. If they cannot find another job, they stay even if they are unhappy. That is why options such as “dissatisfied employees always quit” are wrong.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary bookshop chain, store employees resign one after another. Human resources holds an Exit interview with each person who leaves and sees that most of them give the same reason: the unfair way weekend shifts are shared out. The chain also runs a confidential survey among those who stay and changes the shift system.

soru.q: A survey shows that many software testers at a firm are unhappy and plan to leave, yet a year later almost all are still there because few other jobs exist locally. What does this illustrate?
o: Attitudes predict intentions better than actual behaviour
Attitude surveys never measure feelings in an accurate way
Dissatisfied employees will always quit within one year
Exit interviews are better predictors than attitude surveys
soru.x: Dissatisfaction correctly predicted the intention to leave, but actual behaviour turned out different because there were few alternatives; attitudes predict intentions better than behaviour. The “always quit” option treats this link as absolute, but leaving depends on alternatives.

adimlar.baslik: The interactionist perspective: person-job fit and person-organization fit
adimlar.anlatim:
Do you explain behaviour by personality alone, or by the situation alone? The Interactionist perspective joins the two: behaviour is a function of the interaction between the person and the situation. The same person shines in one setting and fades in another. The idea of “fit” comes from this.

Person-job fit is the match between your knowledge, skills, abilities and other characteristics (KSAO) and the demands of the job. Its question is: do you have what it takes to do this job?

Person-organization fit is the match between your personality, values and goals and the organization. Its question is: does the character of this company suit you?

The two are independent of each other. A skilled accountant meets the demands of the job with ease, but if she is creative and likes risk, she may be unhappy in a company that ties everything to rules. The rule for telling them apart: if skills match the job, it is P-J; if values and personality match the company, it is P-O. The result of good fit is the same in both: employees who are more satisfied, more committed and stay longer.

The SAS Institute case in the textbook shows this: at this company, which appears on Fortune's list of best places to work every year, employee turnover is below 4% while the industry norm is 20%; even Google visited the SAS campus to get ideas.
adimlar.ornek: Yasemin, who believes in sustainability with all her heart but has no kitchen experience, joins an imaginary organic farm restaurant: her Person-organization fit is high, her Person-job fit is low. Murat in the kitchen is a skilled cook, but he does not care about waste and keeps clashing with the restaurant's values: his fit with the job is high, his fit with the organization is low.

soru.q: A talented designer joins a cautious, rule-bound insurance company. She handles every design task with ease, but her love of risk and novelty keeps clashing with the firm's way of doing things. Which fit is weak?
soru.x: Her skills match the demands of the job, so person-job fit is good; what does not match is her personality and the character of the company. The match between personality and values and the organization is person-organization fit. Person-job fit is tempting because the scenario describes a job, but it is only the match between KSAO and job demands.

tuzaklar.yanlis: “Emotional attachment to the company” is job satisfaction.
tuzaklar.dogru: Emotional attachment to the company is Organizational commitment; job satisfaction is the feeling toward the job.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Values matching the company is person-job fit.
tuzaklar.dogru: If values match the company, it is person-organization fit; if skills match the job, it is person-job fit.

tuzaklar.dogru: The method of deciding is unfair, so what is broken is Procedural justice; distributive justice is the fairness of the outcome.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Not knowing your responsibilities is role conflict.
tuzaklar.dogru: This is Role ambiguity; role conflict is demands that are clear but contradict each other.

tuzaklar.dogru: The psychological contract is an unwritten, unspoken expectation on both sides.

tuzaklar.dogru: Attitudes predict intentions; whether someone really leaves depends on alternatives.
