ozet: Attitude: opinions, beliefs and feelings about our environment.
Job satisfaction is the feeling toward the job; organizational commitment is the feeling toward the company.
Sources of positive attitudes: personality and values, job characteristics, justice, psychological contract, relationships, stress.
Distributive justice looks at the outcome, procedural justice at the method, interactional justice at respect.
Role ambiguity is unknown responsibilities; role conflict is contradicting demands.
Surveys work when they are confidential and action follows; an exit interview is held with people who leave.
Attitudes predict intentions better than actual behaviour.
Person-job fit links skills to the job; person-organization fit links values to the company.
lessons.aklinda: What did I get, how was it decided, how was I treated: distributive, procedural, interactional. Skills fit the job, values fit the company.
lessons.sinavda: It comes in Part 1 as multiple-choice questions worth about 4 points. Questions usually give a short employee story and ask which type of justice is broken, which source of stress is at work or which fit is weak. The difference between commitment and satisfaction is also tested often.

lessons.neden: This unit is tested in the case section of the exam: you get a short situation that explains why a person is followed, and you are asked to find the source of the power. Answering by looking at the title is the most common mistake. If you understand the logic of where power comes from, you will catch the right clue in the case.
hedefler: Tell apart formal, informal, designated and emergent leaders.
Identify French and Raven's five sources of power in a case.
Compare position power and personal power and their effects.
Explain how the assumptions of Theory X and Theory Y affect leadership style.
Recognise the models of Tannenbaum and Schmidt and of Muczyk and Reimann.

adimlar.baslik: What is leadership: formal and informal leaders
adimlar.anlatim:
In Chapter 1 you saw the Leading function; this chapter opens it up. Leadership is the act of influencing others to work toward a goal. The definition has no title in it; it has “influencing”. That is why leaders are found at every level of the organization; leadership is not only the job of the person at the very top.

Leaders fall into two groups by the source of their influence. A Formal leader holds a position of authority and is recognised as the official leader. This person can use both the power that comes from the position (position power) and personal power.

An Informal leader has no official position but influences others through personal power. Nobody appointed this person; the group accepts them as its leader. So an informal leader cannot give rewards or hand out punishments; people follow them because of what they know or because they like them.

The distinction rests on this: who made the leader a leader? If the organization gave a position, it is formal; if the group itself accepted the person, it is informal. Both can exist in the same team: on paper the chief is one person, but everyone looks to someone else when a hard question comes up.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary music school, the head of department, Ms Hande, was officially appointed, and she approves the timetable: Formal leader. But when the teachers cannot make up their minds about a new curriculum, they ask the opinion of Riza, an experienced and well-liked piano teacher with no title, and they follow it: Informal leader.

soru.q: In a warehouse team, the shift manager holds the official title, but workers settle disputes by asking a long-serving forklift driver whom everyone trusts, and they follow her advice. What is the forklift driver?
soru.x: She has no official position, but the group accepts her and she influences them through personal power; this is an informal leader. Designated leader is tempting because the team seems to have given her a role, but a designated leader is put in the role by outside forces; here nobody appointed her.

adimlar.baslik: Designated and emergent leaders, and the leadership process
adimlar.anlatim:
You can also group leaders by how they came to lead. A Designated leader is a person put in the role by outside forces: top management sets up a team and puts someone in charge of it. An Emergent leader arises from the dynamics of the group while it works toward a shared goal. Nobody chose this person; as the work goes on, people start turning to them.

This distinction is similar to the formal and informal one, but it is not the same. Formal and informal tell you whether the leader has a position; designated and emergent tell you how the leader became a leader. In the exam, if someone with no title becomes the person everyone turns to during a crisis, the answer “emergent, informal leader” names both correctly at once.

Hollander and Julian describe this relationship as the leadership process: a complex and dynamic exchange relationship built over time between the leader and the followers. The two sides depend on each other to reach a shared goal. So leadership is not a one-way order or a fixed trait you are born with; the relationship grows stronger as followers accept the leader's influence and as the leader gives them something.
adimlar.ornek: On a nature hike, the group's guide Kerem was assigned by the tour company: a designated leader. When fog comes down and the path is lost, Lale, a participant who has walked in these mountains before, reads the map and everyone follows her. Lale is an Emergent leader who arises from the dynamics of the group.

soru.q: During a student hackathon no captain is appointed, but as the night goes on the others start turning to Pieter for direction because he keeps solving blocking problems. How did Pieter become leader?
o: He emerged from the group's dynamics
He was designated by outside forces
He gained legitimate power by title
He was given the figurehead role
soru.x: Nobody appointed him; as the work went on, the group turned to him. This is the definition of an emergent leader. The designated option may be tempting, but a designated leader is put in the role by outside forces; the scenario clearly says no captain was appointed.

adimlar.baslik: Position power: legitimate, reward, coercive
adimlar.anlatim:
If leadership is influence, why are people influenced? French and Raven name five sources of power and split them into two families. The first family is position power: these powers come not from the person but from the chair the person sits in. When the person leaves the chair, the power goes too.

Legitimate power comes from the formal position or title: the “right” to give instructions. Employees listen to the manager because that person is the manager.

Reward power is the ability to give rewards that others want: a bonus, a promotion, a good sales territory.

Coercive power is the ability to punish or to take away something valued: a warning, cutting shifts, taking back a privilege.

Reward and Coercive are like two sides of the same coin; the difference is giving versus taking away. If the person who hits the target gets a bonus, it is reward; if the person who misses it loses the bonus, it is coercive. Legitimate is different from both: people comply not because they expect a reward or a punishment, but simply because “that is the boss”. In the exam, a stress on the title points to legitimate, and incentives such as a bonus or a good territory point to reward.
adimlar.ornek: The regional manager of a pizza chain announces a new delivery rule to the couriers, and they follow it because he is the manager: Legitimate power. He gives the fastest courier of the month an extra day off and the easiest area: Reward power. He takes the evening shifts away from a courier who breaks the rule three times: Coercive power.

soru.q: A hotel manager tells housekeepers that anyone who misses the room-cleaning deadline twice will lose their preferred weekend shifts. Which source of power is she using?
soru.x: She threatens to take away something valued, the preferred weekend shifts; this is Coercive power. Reward power is tempting because the topic is shifts that people want, but reward power means giving something; here there is a threat to take something back.

adimlar.baslik: Personal power: expert and referent
adimlar.anlatim:
The second family is personal power: these powers come from the person, not from the chair. That is why someone with no title can have them too, and they are exactly what informal leaders use.

Expert power comes from having knowledge and skills that others need. The only database expert in the company influences the decisions of top management even without being a manager, because they depend on that person's knowledge.

Referent power comes from being admired: people like you, respect you, and want to be associated with you and to be like you.

The classic exam trap is this: if an expert with no title influences managers, the answer is not legitimate power but expert power. Legitimate power comes only from a formal position. To tell Expert from Referent, look at why people follow: because of what the person knows, or because they like the person and want to be like them? Both can be present in one case; then the right answer is the option that names the two together.
adimlar.ornek: At a sailing club, Vedat is not the club president, but he has been a sailor for twenty years, and he is the one everyone listens to when the wind gets strong: Expert power. The club's young coach Sude is both kind and successful, so the students talk like her and take up every suggestion she makes: Referent power.

soru.q: A data analyst with no managerial title convinces the board to drop a planned acquisition, because only she understands the risk model behind it. Which source of power does she have?
soru.x: What influences the board is knowledge that others need, that is, Expert power. Legitimate power is tempting because a board-level decision is being influenced, but the analyst has no formal managerial position; legitimate power comes only from a position.

adimlar.baslik: The effects of power: which power produces what?
adimlar.anlatim:
Knowing the five powers is not enough; the exam also asks which one produces which result. Build the logic like this: do people join the leader from the inside, or are they forced or bought from the outside?

Coercive power alienates followers. Someone who complies out of fear of punishment complies only while being watched and resents the leader.

Reward power makes people think “how much do I get?” Compliance is tied to the reward; if the reward ends, the effort may drop too.

Referent power creates identification with the leader: because people want to be like the leader, they see the leader's goal as their own.

Expert power and rational arguments create commitment, because people are convinced by their own reasoning that something is right.

The result: the best satisfaction and performance come from referent and expert power. Referent power also strengthens all the other powers; both a bonus and an instruction are received better when they come from a manager people like. That is why options such as “coercive power builds lasting commitment” or “reward power always creates deep commitment” are wrong.
adimlar.ornek: Think of two imaginary bakeries. In the first, the head baker cuts the daily wage of anyone who bakes faulty bread; the apprentices are afraid of him and slack off when he is away. In the second, the head baker explains why the dough has to rest at that temperature; the apprentices are convinced and follow the rule of their own accord. The first bakery shows the alienation that Coercive power causes, the second the commitment that Expert power creates.

soru.q: A new head of a design agency wants her team to truly commit to a new working method rather than merely comply. According to the course, which approach is most likely to work?
o: Explaining the method's logic using her expertise
Paying a bonus to each person who uses the method
Warning that anyone who resists will be demoted
Stating that as head she has the right to decide
soru.x: Expert power and rational arguments create real commitment. The bonus option is tempting, but reward power makes people think “how much do I get?” and ties compliance to the reward; a threat (coercive) alienates, and relying on the title alone (legitimate) is not enough either.

adimlar.baslik: Tannenbaum and Schmidt, Theory X and Theory Y
adimlar.anlatim:
How does a leader use power? Influence-based style models look at how much of the decision authority the leader shares.

The Tannenbaum & Schmidt continuum draws this as a line. At one end is the boss-centred (autocratic) leader, who makes the decision alone. In the middle is the participative leader, who brings employees into the decision. At the other end is the free-rein leader, who leaves the decision largely to the team. Calling it a “continuum” means the styles are not sharp boxes but gradual steps.

How does a leader choose where to stand on this line? According to McGregor, by their assumptions about people. Theory X / Theory Y names these two assumptions. A Theory X leader assumes that people dislike work and must be controlled, so this leader chooses a controlling style and checks everything. A Theory Y leader assumes that people are creative and can direct themselves, so this leader chooses a style that involves them and gives them room to use their own judgement.

Be careful: the theory does not describe a type of employee; it describes the leader's assumption. In the exam, when you see “the manager assumes...”, a need for control points to X and self-motivation points to Y.
adimlar.ornek: Think of two imaginary flower shops. The owner of the first believes the employees will be lazy whenever they get the chance; she approves every bouquet herself and checks on them all day: Theory X, the boss-centred end of the continuum. The owner of the second believes his employees are creative; he leaves the window display to them and only gives ideas: Theory Y, close to the participative end.

soru.q: The owner of a car-wash chain lets each site team design its own work schedule and service ideas, believing that people enjoy responsibility and can motivate themselves. Which assumption guides him?
soru.x: The assumption that people enjoy responsibility and can motivate themselves is Theory Y, and it leads to a participative style. Theory X assumes the exact opposite: people dislike work and must be controlled; the boss-centred style is the product of that assumption.

adimlar.baslik: Muczyk and Reimann's four styles
adimlar.anlatim:
Tannenbaum and Schmidt draw a single line. Muczyk and Reimann split leadership into four styles, and the names of these styles answer two separate questions at once.

The second word of the name tells you about the decision: an autocrat makes the decision alone, a democrat shares the decision with employees. The first word of the name tells you about the execution: a directive leader closely directs how the work is done, while a permissive leader gives employees freedom in carrying it out. Put the two together and you get four styles:

  • Directive autocrat: makes the decision alone and also closely directs the execution.
  • Permissive autocrat: makes the decision alone but leaves the execution to employees.
  • Directive democrat: makes the decision together with employees but closely directs the execution.
  • Permissive democrat: shares both the decision and the execution (decisions and execution).

The notes describe only the permissive democrat in so many words; you can build the other three yourself from these two parts of the names. Do not confuse this model with Theory X / Y: X and Y are the leader's assumptions, while Muczyk and Reimann's four styles name the leader's behaviour.
adimlar.ornek: Ozan, the editor of a school newspaper, decides which stories will be published by voting with the team, and he leaves it to each reporter to decide how to write their story. Because he shares both the decision and the execution, he is a permissive democrat. If he chose the stories himself and also dictated the way of writing line by line, he would be a directive autocrat.

soru.q: A football club's youth coach lets the players vote on the season's training focus and then leaves it to them to organise how they practise it. Which Muczyk and Reimann style fits best?
soru.x: The decision is shared through a vote (democrat) and the execution is also left to the players (permissive); because both decision and execution are shared, this is the permissive democrat. Directive democrat is tempting because the decision is again made together, but in that style the coach would closely direct the execution.

tuzaklar.yanlis: An expert with no title who influences managers has legitimate power.
tuzaklar.dogru: Power that comes from knowledge is Expert power; legitimate power comes only from a formal position.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Giving a bonus and a good territory to those who hit the target is referent power.
tuzaklar.dogru: Giving rewards is Reward power; referent power comes from admiration and identification.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A person who is liked and seen as a role model uses expert power.
tuzaklar.dogru: If people like the person and want to be like them, it is Referent power.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Coercive power creates lasting commitment.
tuzaklar.dogru: Coercive power alienates; real commitment comes from expert power and rational argument.

tuzaklar.yanlis: An informal leader is appointed from outside the group.
tuzaklar.dogru: A leader appointed from outside is designated; an informal leader has no position and is accepted by the group.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Theory X and Theory Y are two types of employee.
tuzaklar.dogru: Both are the leader's assumption about people: X is control, Y is self-direction.

ozet: Leadership is influencing others toward a goal, and it is found at every level.
A formal leader leads through a position; an informal leader leads because the group accepts them.
A designated leader comes from outside; an emergent leader arises from the dynamics of the group.
The leadership process: a two-way, dynamic exchange relationship built over time.
Position power: legitimate, reward, coercive. Personal power: expert, referent.
Coercive power alienates, expert power creates commitment, referent power strengthens the others.
Theory X rests on the assumption of control, Theory Y on the assumption of involvement.
The Tannenbaum and Schmidt line: boss-centred, participative, free-rein.
Muczyk and Reimann: autocrat/democrat describes the decision, directive/permissive the execution.
lessons.aklinda: Three powers come with the chair: the right, the carrot and the stick (legitimate, reward, coercive). Two powers come with the person: knowledge and admiration (expert, referent).

The case explains why a person is followed and asks you to find the source of power or the type of leader; look at where the influence comes from, not at the title.

lessons.ad: Trait and behavioural approaches to leadership
lessons.neden: Leadership research began with two simple questions: is it who leaders are that makes them leaders, or what they do? Understanding these two approaches and their limits helps you name a leader's behaviour correctly in cases, and it protects you from the traps the exam likes, such as the “friendly but task-focused” leader.
hedefler: Explain the question the trait approach asks and its limit.
List Kirkpatrick and Locke's core leadership traits.
Name the trait with the strongest link to leadership according to Judge and colleagues.
Tell apart task-oriented and people-oriented behaviour in a case.
Match the three decision-making styles to their results.

adimlar.baslik: Who is a leader? The trait approach
adimlar.anlatim:
The first question of leadership research was this: are some people born to be leaders? The Trait approach looks for the personal traits that make someone a leader. This approach began with Stogdill: which physical, personality and social traits set leaders apart?

Later, Kirkpatrick & Locke identified the core traits that give leadership potential. This is the list: Drive, that is, high effort, ambition, energy, persistence and initiative; leadership motivation, that is, the wish to lead others; honesty and integrity; self-confidence; cognitive ability; knowledge of the business. Charisma, creativity and flexibility are also mentioned in addition to these.

Pay attention to the word “potential”. These traits give a person the chance to lead, but they do not guarantee success. A person may have strong drive; if they do not know the business or nobody trusts them, they still cannot lead. When this list is asked in the exam, cross out options that include physical and social traits such as height, age or wealth, or soft traits such as “modesty, conflict avoidance”.
adimlar.ornek: In a student theatre club, Arda, a candidate for president, is the first to arrive at rehearsal and the last to leave, and he sets out to solve every problem himself: high Drive. But if he does not understand stage work and has lost trust because he does not keep his promises, this potential is not enough. That is why the Trait approach sees traits as potential, not as a guarantee.

soru.q: A panel choosing team captains rates candidates only on energy, ambition, honesty, self-confidence, intelligence and knowledge of the business. Which approach to leadership is the panel using?
soru.x: The panel rates candidates by the personal traits they have, and the list matches Kirkpatrick and Locke's core traits; this is the trait approach. The behavioural approach is tempting, but it looks at what a leader does; here the panel looks at who the person is.

adimlar.baslik: Traits linked to leadership and the limit of the approach
adimlar.anlatim:
Judge et al. looked at which traits are really linked to leadership. The findings connect with the personality traits from Chapter 2:

  • Intelligence: a positive but modest link. According to Goleman, IQ is a threshold; what separates the good from the great is Emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ means monitoring your own emotions and the emotions of others and using them to guide your behaviour; its elements are self-awareness, motivation, empathy and social skills.
  • Extraversion: the trait with the strongest link to emerging as a leader and being effective.
  • Conscientiousness and openness: these people emerge as leaders more often and are more effective.
  • Agreeableness: modest people who avoid conflict are seen as leaders less often.
  • Self-esteem and integrity: they help leaders; lost integrity harms both the leader and the company.
  • Self-monitoring: high self-monitors emerge as leaders more often.

The limit of the approach has two sides. Traits matter more in small, flexible firms than in rule-bound firms; and the approach ignores the situation. In short, leaders are not just “born”.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary software team, Cem has the highest IQ, but he does not notice who is tense in meetings and he hurts the team. Seda is a little less brilliant than he is, but she reads her colleagues' feelings and adjusts how she speaks, and she pulls the team together. Both have passed the intelligence threshold; Emotional intelligence (EQ) makes the difference.

soru.q: Two equally intelligent shift managers are compared. One notices her staff's frustration and adjusts how she speaks to them; the other ignores moods. According to Goleman, what mostly separates the better leader?
o: Emotional intelligence, since IQ is only a threshold
IQ, since intelligence is the main driver of success
Agreeableness, since avoiding conflict builds trust
Self-efficacy, since belief in a task drives results
soru.x: According to Goleman, IQ is a threshold; when both have passed it, what sets the good leader apart is monitoring emotions and adjusting behaviour to them, that is, EQ. The IQ option is tempting, but intelligence is given as equal in the scenario, and Goleman also says IQ alone does not make the difference.

adimlar.baslik: What does a leader do? Task-oriented and people-oriented behaviour
adimlar.anlatim:
When the trait approach could not give a satisfying answer, researchers changed the question: not who leaders are, but what they do. The studies at Ohio State and Michigan found two kinds of behaviour.

Task-oriented behaviour is also known as initiating structure: structuring roles, giving instructions and deadlines, focusing on performance and goals. Its result is slightly higher productivity; but too much of it leads to burnout.

People-oriented behaviour is also known as consideration: showing interest in employees' feelings, treating them with respect, caring about their well-being. Its result is more satisfied and more positive employees.

The exam trap is this: if a friendly leader hands out roles, sets deadlines and checks results, the behaviour is task-oriented. What counts is what the leader does, not the leader's personality or manner. Also, these two behaviours are not opposites; a leader can do both. The rule: if the leader deals with the structure of the work, it is task-oriented; if the leader deals with the person, it is people-oriented.
adimlar.ornek: Pelin, who runs an animal shelter, hands out the dog-walking list to the volunteers every Monday, sets the time for each job and checks on Friday who has done what: Task-oriented behaviour. The same Pelin notices that a volunteer is sad about the death of an old dog, and she sits down and talks with them: People-oriented behaviour.

soru.q: A cheerful, well-liked IT team lead jokes with everyone, but her main activities are assigning tickets, setting due dates and reviewing each person's closed tickets every evening. Which behaviour dominates?
soru.x: Assigning work, setting due dates and checking results are task-oriented behaviour; the fact that the leader is cheerful and well liked does not change this. People-oriented is tempting because the mood is warm, but people-oriented behaviour means showing interest in feelings and well-being; the main activities in the scenario are not that.

adimlar.baslik: Decision-making styles
adimlar.anlatim:
The behavioural approach also looks at how leaders make decisions. There are three styles, and the difference between them is who holds the decision.

Authoritarian decision-making: the leader makes the decision alone and announces it to the team.

Democratic decision-making: employees take part in the decision. Its result is more satisfaction, because people feel that their voice is heard.

Laissez-faire decision-making: employees make the decision themselves, with very little guidance from the leader. This style has the worst record: it leads to role ambiguity and conflict. Remember from Chapter 2: when nobody knows who will do what, stress goes up.

Do not confuse laissez-faire with democratic. In the democratic style the leader is inside the process and draws employees into the decision; in laissez-faire the leader steps away. Do not confuse this style with people-oriented behaviour either: laissez-faire is a decision-making style, that is, leaving the work to the team; it is not showing interest in people.
adimlar.ornek: The owner of a kebab shop sets the new prices himself and puts them up on the wall: Authoritarian decision-making. The next month he votes with the employees on which dessert to add: Democratic decision-making. When he goes on holiday, he says “sort out the shifts among yourselves” and leaves no guidance at all; two employees want the same day and an argument breaks out: Laissez-faire decision-making.

soru.q: A museum director asks her curators to choose next year's exhibitions, joins their meetings, discusses the options with them and accepts the group's choice. Which decision-making style is this?
soru.x: The leader is inside the process and employees take part in the decision; this is Democratic. Laissez-faire is tempting because the curators make the choice, but in that style the leader steps away and gives almost no guidance; here she joins the meetings and discusses the options.

adimlar.baslik: The shared limit of the two approaches
adimlar.anlatim:
The trait and behavioural approaches ask different questions but stumble at the same point: both ignore the effect of the situation. They do not say which trait or which behaviour works under which conditions.

You can see this clearly in the findings on behaviour. Task-oriented behaviour raises productivity a little, but too much of it brings burnout; people-oriented behaviour raises satisfaction. Democratic decisions raise satisfaction, while laissez-faire has the worst record. Every behaviour has a gain and a price; so no style works everywhere. The same is true for traits: the notes say traits matter more in small, flexible firms than in rule-bound firms; so even a trait gains its value from the context.

In the exam this limit comes in two forms. The first is direct: “What is the main limit of the two approaches?” The answer: they ignore the situation. The second is through wrong options with absolute wording: “always leads to the highest satisfaction”, “guarantees effective leadership”. Be suspicious when you see an absolute claim; the basic idea of this lesson is that there is no single recipe in leadership that fits everywhere.
adimlar.ornek: An imaginary company first sends Nil, an energetic and self-confident supervisor, to a warehouse where every step is set by regulations; there is no room to take initiative there, so she cannot make a difference. Then it sends her to a small, flexible design studio; there the same traits carry the team along. What changed is not the person but the situation; neither approach takes this effect of the situation into account.

soru.q: A consultant tells a retail chain: 'Train all store managers to be people-oriented and democratic, and they will be effective in every store.' What is the main weakness of this advice?
o: It ignores the situation in which each manager leads
It ignores the traits that managers are born with
It ignores the value of laissez-faire decision-making
It ignores that task focus always lowers productivity
soru.x: The main limit of both the trait and the behavioural approach is that they ignore the situation; no style works everywhere. The inborn-traits option may be tempting, but the notes say leaders are not just “born”; and task focus does not lower productivity, it raises it a little.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A friendly leader who gives out roles and deadlines is people-oriented.
tuzaklar.dogru: Roles, deadlines and checking are task-oriented behaviour; what counts is the work done, not the manner.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Laissez-faire is a people-oriented style.
tuzaklar.dogru: Laissez-faire is a decision-making style: leaving the decision to the team. Showing interest in people is people-oriented behaviour.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Agreeableness is the trait with the strongest link to leadership.
tuzaklar.dogru: The strongest link is with Extraversion; agreeable people who avoid conflict are seen as leaders less often.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A high IQ guarantees success as a leader.
tuzaklar.dogru: According to Goleman, IQ is a threshold; EQ makes the difference.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Laissez-faire has the best record because it gives employees freedom.
tuzaklar.dogru: It has the worst record: it brings role ambiguity and conflict.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The democratic style and laissez-faire are the same, since employees decide in both.
tuzaklar.dogru: In the democratic style the leader takes part in the process; in laissez-faire the leader gives very little guidance and steps back.

ozet: The trait approach asks “who is a leader?” and began with Stogdill.
Kirkpatrick and Locke: drive, leadership motivation, honesty, self-confidence, cognitive ability, knowledge of the business.
The trait with the strongest link to leadership is extraversion.
According to Goleman, IQ is a threshold and emotional intelligence makes the difference.
Task-oriented behaviour builds structure; people-oriented behaviour shows interest in feelings and well-being.
In the authoritarian style the leader decides alone, in the democratic style employees take part in the decision, and in the laissez-faire style the team decides without guidance.
Laissez-faire has the worst record.
The shared limit of the two approaches: they ignore the situation.
lessons.aklinda: The trait approach asks “who?”, the behavioural approach asks “what do they do?”; both forget to ask “where?”
lessons.sinavda: It comes in the short cases of Part 2, worth about 4 points. The case describes a leader's daily behaviour and asks whether it is task-oriented or people-oriented, or asks for the decision-making style; sometimes the shared limit of the two approaches is asked too.
